claim: French wheat flour types are defined by ash on dry matter: T45 below 0.50 %, T55 0.50–0.60 %, T65 0.62–0.75 %, T80 0.75–0.90 %, T110 1.00–1.20 %, T150 above 1.40 %. These six types were homologated in 1963 and replace the obligatory statement of the ash content.
conditions: soft wheat flour sold in France; ash on dry matter ("% ramené à la matière sèche")

source.locator: p. 3, 'Définition des types de farine' table
source.author: FranceAgriMer

notes: Same six ranges in the 2024 miller circular (ANMF/CNBPF) and in Bourre et al. 2008 Table 1 ('Réglementation de 1963'). The ranges leave gaps (0.60–0.62, 0.90–1.00, 1.20–1.40 %) that belong to no type.

claim: T130 wheat flour is not one of the six regulatory French types; it is sold as wholemeal ('farine complète') flour with ash of about 1.2–1.4 %, filling the gap between T110 and T150.
notes: The miller circular (ANMF 2024) lists only T45, T55, T65, T80, T110 and T150 for wheat, so T130 is a trade name; the Wikipedia table gives 1.2–1.4 % but cites only the 1963 text, which has six types.

claim: French rye (and méteil) flour types are T70 (ash 0.60–1.00 %), T85 (0.75–1.25 %), T130 (1.20–1.50 %) and T170 (above 1.50 %); the ranges overlap. Méteil flour today means an equal-parts blend of wheat and rye flour.

source.locator: p. 1, second table ('Taux de cendres de la farine de seigle et de méteil'); p. 2 'Qu'est-ce que la farine de méteil'
source.author: ANMF / CNBPF

notes: The circular prints 'Type 13' for T130 (typo) and does not state the moisture basis for rye; the wheat types are on dry matter (FranceAgriMer 2012).

claim: In a 2010 survey of French mills, T65 made up 66 % of conventional bread-making flour and T55 32 %; in organic bread-making flour T80 and T110 made up 33 % each, and T55 plus T65 only 24 %. Flour for 'pain de tradition française' may contain only bread-making wheat flours, wheat gluten, α-amylases, wheat malt flour, soy flour and fava-bean flour (decree of 13 September 1993); it was 7 % of conventional flour.
conditions: 165 responding mills, 2010 deliveries to bread making

source.locator: p. 3 ('Définition des types de farine', tradition ingredients); p. 7 ('Types de farine dans le secteur de la panification', 'Farine pour pain de tradition')
source.author: FranceAgriMer

claim: Pooled French flours analysed by an accredited lab: T55 moisture 13.9 %, ash 0.5 % DM, protein 11.7 %, total fibre 3.9 %; T65 (tradition) 13.2 / 0.6 / 11.6 / 4.3; T80 13.5 / 0.7 / 11.4 / 5.0; T110 (organic) 12.5 / 1.1 / 11.7 / 5.7; T150 12.7 / 1.6 / 11.9 / 12.5; rye T130 11.8 / 1.5 / 9.1 / 11.7.
conditions: blends of 5–10 commercial flours per type from mills in several regions; protein Kjeldahl N × 6.25 as is (g/100 g); fibre AOAC 985.29 (g/100 g)

source.author: Bourre et al.

notes: Protein differs little between wheat types (about 11.5 g/100 g); fibre is about tripled from T55 to T150. N × 6.25 gives values about 9 % higher than the N × 5.7 used for wheat elsewhere.

claim: Reference French bread recipes validated by a committee of bakers and millers use 62 % water for T55 and for T65 everyday baguette, 68 % for T65 'tradition' (0.8 % yeast, 150 min bulk), 64 % for a T65 levain bread, 66 % for T80 and for an organic T110 levain bread, and 70 % for a T150 wholemeal boule.
conditions: spiral or oblique-axis mixer, dough 24–25 °C; baker's percentages

source.locator: Annexe 'Recettes et protocoles de fabrication des pains', p. 72
source.author: Bourre et al.

notes: Same flour (T65) takes 62 % in a short straight dough and 68 % in the long-fermented tradition dough: process, not only flour, sets bread hydration.

claim: The same study is internally inconsistent about its rye bread: the text describes 66 % rye T130 + 34 % wheat T65, while the recipe annex lists rye T85 66 + wheat T65 33 with 65 % water and 1 % added gluten; a farmhouse bread with 10 % rye T130 took 68 % water in the final dough.

source.locator: Matériel et méthodes ('pain de seigle (66 % farine de seigle T130 + 34 % farine de blé T65)') vs Annexe (suite), p. 73
source.author: Bourre et al.

claim: Ciqual 2020 (as-is values) gives for French wheat flours: T45 water 11.3 %, protein 9.94 % (N × 6.25; 9.06 with the Jones factor), fibre 2.5 %, ash 0.48 %; T55 12.5 / 9.9 (9.03) / 3.2 / 0.54; T80 10.7 / 10.9 (9.95) / 4.2 / 0.74; T110 12.4 / 10.3 (9.61) / 6.8 / 1.09; T150 10.7 / 12.2 (11.4) / 10.2 / 1.31. Its T65 row (protein 14.9 %, ash 1.06 % as is) is inconsistent with the T65 ash range.
notes: T65 ash 1.06 % as is = 1.22 % on dry matter, outside 0.62–0.75 %: treat that row as unreliable. Compared with Bourre et al. 2008 the Ciqual T55 protein (9.9 %) is lower than the pooled mill average (11.7 %).

claim: Ciqual 2020 gives for French rye flours (as is): T85 water 12 %, protein 8.7 % (N × 6.25), fibre 7.15 %, ash 0.69 %; T130 9.9 / 7.76 / 9.5 / 1.38; T170 10.8 / 17.1 / 23.8 / 2.5. The T170 row matches the USDA 'rye flour, dark' entry (protein 15.91 %, fibre 23.8 %, ash 2.5 %, water 10.75 %), so it is borrowed US data rather than a French analysis.
conditions: g/100 g as sold; Ciqual codes 9532, 9533, 9530
notes: Bourre et al. 2008 measured 9.1 % protein and 11.7 % fibre for pooled rye T130 (science-flour-0005).

claim: Ciqual 2020 (as is) gives buckwheat flour 11.5 % protein, 4.2 % fibre, 1.65 % ash; maize flour 6.23 / 2.55 / 0.53; rice flour 8.0 / 3.3 / 1.27; barley flour 10.6 / 8.85 / 1.39; chestnut flour 6.1 / 12.6 / 2.34 with only 5.5 % water and 46.9 % starch; spelt flour 12.5 / 9.3 / 1.47; raw durum semolina 12.0 / 3.37 / 0.78.
conditions: g/100 g as sold; protein N × 6.25
notes: The spelt row (ash 1.47 % as is) is a high-extraction or wholemeal spelt flour.

claim: DIN 10355 types wheat flour by mineral (ash) content on dry matter: 405 at most 0.50 %, 550 0.51–0.63 %, 812 0.64–0.90 %, 1050 0.91–1.20 %, 1600 1.21–1.80 %; durum flour 1600 1.55–1.85 %; wheat Backschrot 1700 (meal without germ) at most 2.10 %. The type number is the mean mineral content in mg per 100 g dry matter.
conditions: Germany, DIN 10355:2007-11; ash in % of dry matter

source.locator: section 'Typisierung in Deutschland nach DIN', table 'Mehltypen nach DIN 10355'
source.author: Wikipedia (transcription of DIN 10355)

claim: DIN 10355 rye types: 815 at most 0.90 % ash (dry matter), 997 0.91–1.10 %, 1150 1.11–1.30 %, 1370 1.31–1.60 %, 1740 1.61–1.80 %; 1800 is Roggenbackschrot, a meal without germ, at most 2.20 %. Wholemeal products keep the germ and get no type number.

source.locator: table 'Mehltypen nach DIN 10355', Roggen rows; paragraph below the table
source.author: Wikipedia (transcription of DIN 10355)

notes: Rye 1150 and 1370 are described as the typical bakers' flours for rye and mixed rye breads.

claim: DIN 10355 spelt types: 630 at most 0.70 % ash (usable like wheat 550), 812 0.71–0.90 %, 1050 0.91–1.20 %.

Italian law (DPR 187/2001, art. 1) sets soft-wheat bread flours, on 100 parts dry matter: type 00 ash at most 0.55 % and protein at least 9.00 %; type 0 at most 0.65 % and 11.00 %; type 1 at most 0.80 % and 12.00 %; type 2 at most 0.95 % and 12.00 %; farina integrale ash 1.30–1.70 % and protein at least 12.00 %; moisture at most 14.50 % (15.50 % if labelled).
conditions: protein N × 5.70; applies to flours for bread making (art. 1 c. 4)
notes: Secondary tables that put 00 at ash ≤ 0.50 % do not match the decree text, which allows 0.55 %.

claim: Italian durum products (DPR 187/2001, art. 2), on dry matter: semola ash at most 0.90 %, protein at least 10.50 %, and at most 25 % of it may pass a 0.180 mm sieve; semolato 0.90–1.35 % ash, protein ≥ 11.50 %; semola integrale 1.40–1.80 %; farina di grano duro 1.36–1.70 %. Re-milled semola and semolato ('rimacinati') are allowed only for bread making and retail.
notes: Semola rimacinata has no separate ash limit: it is re-milled semola (≤ 0.90 %) or semolato.

claim: US 'flour' (21 CFR 137.105) is not typed by ash: its ash, on a moisture-free basis, may not exceed one twentieth of its protein (moisture-free) plus 0.35; moisture is at most 15 % and at least 98 % must pass a 212 µm sieve. All-purpose and bread flour are not separate standards of identity.
notes: Worked: 12 % protein (moisture-free) allows ash up to 12/20 + 0.35 = 0.95 %. Part 137 has no 'bread flour' or 'all-purpose flour' section.

claim: US whole wheat flour (21 CFR 137.200) keeps the proportions of all natural constituents of the wheat other than moisture; at least 90 % must pass a 2.36 mm sieve and at least 50 % an 850 µm sieve; moisture at most 15 %.

US semolina (21 CFR 137.320) is durum wheat ground so that it passes a No. 20 sieve with at most 3 % through a No. 100 sieve, with ash at most 0.92 % (moisture-free); durum flour (137.220) allows ash up to 1.5 %.

USDA SR Legacy (as is): all-purpose wheat flour 10.33 % protein, 0.47 % ash, 2.7 % fibre, 11.92 % water; bread flour 11.98 / 0.47 / 2.4 / 13.36; whole-grain wheat flour 13.21 / 1.58 / 10.7 / 10.74; cake flour 8.2 / 0.39 / 1.7; 'industrial 15 % protein' flour 15.33 / 0.53 / 2.4.

USDA SR Legacy (as is) for other milled grains: rye flour light 9.82 % protein / 0.78 % ash / 8.0 % fibre, medium 10.88 / 1.2 / 11.8, dark 15.91 / 2.5 / 23.8; spelt grain 14.57 / 1.78 / 10.7; Kamut khorasan grain 14.54 / 1.67 / 11.1; semolina 12.68 / 0.77 / 3.9; buckwheat whole-groat flour 12.62 / 2.54 / 10.0; oat flour (partly debranned) 14.66 / 1.97 / 6.5; barley flour 10.5 / 1.28 / 10.1; whole-grain corn flour 6.93 / 1.45 / 7.3; degermed corn flour 5.59 / 0.46 / 1.9; white rice flour 5.95 / 0.61 / 2.4; brown rice flour 7.23 / 1.54 / 4.6; dried unpeeled European chestnuts 6.39 / 2.4 / 11.7.
conditions: g/100 g as [protein, ash, total dietary fibre]
notes: Spelt and khorasan entries are whole grains, i.e. wholemeal flour.

claim: US bread flour is a high-protein patent flour from hard red spring or winter wheat with 11.5–13.5 % protein (also given as 12–14 %, against about 11 % for all-purpose flour); all-purpose flour is milled from hard red wheat or an 80:20 hard:soft blend.
conditions: US commercial classes (protein on 14 % moisture basis)

source.locator: 'What is Bread Flour?' and 'Function'; all-purpose-flour page 'What is'
source.author: BAKERpedia

notes: The page itself gives both ranges.

claim: A large US miller specifies its bread flour at 12.7 % protein, its all-purpose flour at 11.7 % and its high-gluten flour (hard red spring wheat, for bagels and hearth breads) at 14 %.

source.locator: bread flour and high-gluten flour product pages, 'Why you'll love it'
source.author: King Arthur Baking Company

notes: One brand; used only to place the US classes.

claim: Across 15 cultivars per species grown at four German sites (n = 60 each), the gliadin/glutenin ratio averaged 2.5 in common wheat, 3.3 in spelt, 4.0 in durum, 4.9 in emmer and 6.5 in einkorn; mean glutenin content fell from 16.6 (common wheat) and 19.0 mg/g (spelt) to 12.8 (emmer) and 10.3 mg/g (einkorn). Common wheat had the lowest protein (mean 96.1 mg/g) and durum the highest (120.7 mg/g).
conditions: wholemeal flours; protein Dumas N × 5.7; gliadin/glutenin by Bradford assay
notes: A higher gliadin/glutenin ratio means softer, more extensible, less elastic dough; common wheat literature range 1.5–3.1.

claim: Gluten usually makes up 80–90 % of the protein of white wheat flour; in wholemeal flours it was 60–80 %, because albumins and globulins from the outer layers add non-gluten protein.
notes: Consequence for calculators: wholemeal protein overstates gluten-forming protein.

claim: Wholemeal flours (dry basis) of einkorn averaged 14.6 % protein, 2.2 % ash and 15.1 % total dietary fibre; emmer 14.5 / 2.2 / 19.1; spelt 15.2 / 2.1 / 17.3; North-Dakota hard red spring wheat 17.3 / 2.2 / 19.2. The hulled wheats had more fat (1.6–2.3 %) than the bread wheat (1.1 %).
conditions: 3–4 genotypes per hulled species, 8 HRS genotypes; TDF by AOAC 2011.25 (includes oligosaccharides)
notes: The authors note lower values (11.1–11.6 % protein) for German-grown einkorn, emmer and spelt in other work: protein depends on growing conditions.

claim: In 90 spelt genotypes, white-flour farinograph water absorption averaged 55.95 % (SD 2.07, range 51.3–63.3 %) against 62.9 % and 60.0 % for two bread-wheat controls; gluten index averaged 59.3 (wheat controls 97.3 and 99.7); wholemeal protein averaged 18.99 % (12.17–22.20 %) and falling number 383 s (103–613 s).
conditions: Hungarian trials; farinograph ICC 115/1 on laboratory-milled flour (flour yield ~58 %)
notes: High protein and gluten content did not mean good gluten quality: spelt gluten is more extensible and less stable.

claim: Stone-milled flours of six Italian common-wheat varieties (several ancient) had alveograph W 47–87 × 10⁻⁴ J, farinograph water absorption 52.3–59.0 % and falling numbers 313–440 s; khorasan semolato had W 57, P/L 1.6, absorption 55.8 %, falling number 591 s, 10.45 % protein and 1.345 % ash (dry matter); durum 'Senatore Cappelli' semolato had W 55, absorption 62.0 %, falling number 473 s, 12.90 % protein, 1.57 % ash. All T. turgidum samples had gluten index below 10 %.
conditions: organic stone-milled flour and semolato; protein Dumas N × 5.7
notes: All flours were classed as weak.

claim: Stone-milled flours of three southern-Italian ancient wheats at 72 % (type 0), 80 % (type 1) and 100 % extraction (integrale) absorbed 54.7–64.9 %, 56.7–63.8 % and 57.1–66.0 % water on the farinograph; absorption rose from type 0 to wholemeal in two of three varieties; stability was only 1.6–3.1 min and protein 8.06–10.54 %.
notes: Variety moved absorption more (up to 10 points) than sifting degree (1–4 points).

claim: Finely micronized (< 160 µm) wholemeal flours had back-calculated farinograph water absorption of 87.4 % (wheat), 83.4 % (rye), 76.4 % (spelt), 70.6 % (barley), 63.8 % (sorghum) and 63.4 % (buckwheat), against 60.6 % for a white wheat flour type 530; their falling numbers were 324, 200, 238, 389, 398 and 918 s (white flour 320 s).
conditions: absorption measured on 50:50 blends with the T530 flour and recalculated for the wholemeal flour (AACC 54-21), n = 2
notes: Micronization damages starch and raises absorption; the recalculation assumes blend absorption is additive. Buckwheat's very high falling number means very little α-amylase.

claim: At practical dough firmness and 14 % flour moisture, an industry handbook gives water per 100 flour of 60–62 for wheat bread, 55–57 for wheat rolls, 62–66 for 90/10 wheat/rye, 66–70 for 80/20, 68–72 for 70/30, 70–74 for 60/40 and 50/50, 72–76 for 40/60 rye-rich, 76–80 for 70/30 rye/wheat, 78–82 for 80/20, 80–84 for 90/10, 82–86 for 100 % rye bread and 84–88 for coarse rye bread; water binding rises with extraction rate.

source.locator: table 'Water absorption of different ratios of flour mixture'
source.author: IREKS GmbH

notes: Rye-rich doughs are made far softer than wheat doughs: 82–86 % against 60–62 %.

claim: Usual net dough yields (TA = 100 + water per 100 flour) are 176–180 for wholemeal and meal doughs, 175–178 for rye bread, 170–175 for ciabatta, 165 for baguette, 154–158 for wheat and toast bread, 156–158 for rolls and 150 for pretzels; poolish is about TA 200.

source.locator: table 'Ungefähre Netto-TAs sind bei Teigen üblich' (citing Loderbauer 2008)
source.author: Wikipedia (table from Loderbauer, Das Bäckerbuch in Lernfeldern)

notes: TA 165 = 65 % hydration.

claim: For wheat flour type 550 a falling number of 300–360 s is normal; 240–300 s gives faster development, slightly damp doughs and stronger colour, 360–420 s weak proof, pale crust and small volume. For rye 997 and 1150 the normal band is 180–240 s; 120–180 s gives damp, flat bread with an irregular crumb, 240–300 s round, pale, dry-crumbed bread that stales early.

source.locator: tables 'Dough and baked goods properties ... depending on the falling number'
source.author: IREKS GmbH

notes: Falling number is an indirect, inverse measure of α-amylase activity.

claim: Hybrid rye varieties grown since the 1970s resist sprouting and are poorer in enzymes than older ryes; today's rye flours absorb up to 10 % more water than those of 60 years ago, and low enzyme activity now causes small volume, dry crumb with tears and poor keeping more often than excess activity does. Rye bread doughs should stay at or below 28 °C.

Light (55 % extraction) rye flours from seven Polish cultivars had 0.55–1.01 % ash and 5.3–6.1 % protein (dry matter), dietary fibre 6.24–8.63 %, Mixolab water absorption 59.0–68.6 % and falling numbers 215–343 s; the authors cite 63.8–70.6 % absorption for wholemeal rye.
conditions: organic rye, 2019–2020 harvests; WA by Mixolab (ISO 17718)
notes: Year means for protein (7.9 and 6.2 %) printed in the paper fall outside its own stated range.

claim: Hard red spring wheat flours on a 14 % moisture basis: stone-milled refined flour absorbed 68.93 % on the farinograph (starch damage 7.72 %), roller-milled refined 65.98 % (6.33 %), stone-milled wholemeal 74.45 % and roller-milled wholemeal 73.99 %; baking absorption was 71.16, 68.34, 79.17 and 78.32 % respectively.
conditions: AACCI 54-21.02, 500 BU, all on 14 % moisture basis
notes: Wholemeal added 5.5–8.0 points of farinograph absorption and 8–10 points of baking absorption over the refined flour of the same mill type.

claim: Flours can be classed by farinograph absorption: very strong above 63 % (development > 10 min, MTI < 10 FU), strong above 58 % (4–8 min, 15–50 FU), medium 54–60 % (2.5–4 min, 60–100 FU) and weak below 55 % (< 2.5 min, > 100 FU). Absorption rises with protein, damaged starch, pentosans and added vital gluten and falls with higher flour moisture and with sprouting or high amylase.

source.locator: 'Influencing factors' and 'Classification of flour according to its water absorption'
source.author: BAKERpedia

notes: Cites Serna-Saldivar 2010 for the classification.

claim: Damaged starch is 1–4 % of total starch in soft-wheat flour and 6–12 % in hard-wheat (HRS, HRW) flour; damaged granules absorb 2–3 times more water than intact ones, which take up about 40 % of their weight. A falling number of 250–300 s is considered ideal for bread flour.
notes: IREKS gives 300–360 s as normal for type 550 (science-flour-0032): the 'ideal' falling number differs between sources.

claim: In 18 hard red spring wheat flour composites starch damage ranged 5.90–7.00 %, considered moderate and suited to bread; damage above about 8 % can disrupt gluten network formation through competition for water. Ash correlated with farinograph absorption (r = 0.570) and protein with absorption (r = 0.416).
conditions: US hard red spring wheat supply-chain samples

claim: For whole wheat flour add about 5 g of liquid per 120 g cup of flour because bran absorbs water, and lengthen the rest; blending one-quarter to one-half part whole wheat with one part bread flour is suggested.
notes: 5/120 = +4.2 baker's points; measured farinograph gaps are larger (+5.5 to +8 points, science-flour-0035).

claim: Spelt flour has lower water absorption than bread flour: replacing 50 % of bread flour with spelt may need about 10 % less added water for better loaf volume; spelt is quoted at 12–15 % protein and 10–15 % crude fibre (wholegrain).
notes: Consistent with the 6-point lower farinograph absorption of spelt in Tóth et al. 2022 (science-flour-0026).

claim: Einkorn gives quicker mixing, lower volume and a yellow crumb (carotenoids); when it replaces flour in a recipe the liquid may need to be cut by roughly 15–20 %.
notes: No farinograph value for einkorn was found in the sources read; this rule is the only absorption figure.

claim: Buckwheat flour needs more water and mixing time than wheat when used in recipes, and about 30 % of the flour is the upper substitution threshold in bread.

Flour strength (alveograph W) maps to bread hydration and fermentation length: W 0–150 about 50 % water, very short fermentation (cookies); W 150–250 50–60 %, short to medium; W 250–350 60–70 %, long; W above 350 70–90 %, very long.
notes: Basis for the cold-retard classes in model-flour.json: stronger flour, longer tolerable fermentation.

claim: Spelt and wheat doughs (more than 70 % of the flour) can be kneaded, stretched and folded and shaped; rye, emmer, einkorn, rice and corn doughs are only homogenized, without kneading, folding or shaping.

A sourdough handbook equates flour labels across countries: cake flour = T405 = T45 = 00; all-purpose = T550 = T55 = 0; bread flour = T405 or T550 = T45 or T55 = 00 or 0; T812 = T80 = 1; T1050 = T110 = 2; whole = Vollkorn = T150 = integrale. By the ash limits of the standards these are approximate: Italian 0 (≤ 0.65 %) spans French T55 and the lower T65, and German 812 (0.64–0.90 %) spans T65 and T80.
notes: Disagreement between a creator table and the standards' ash ranges; US classes are protein classes and have no ash equivalent.

claim: Under EU law 'gluten' is a protein fraction from wheat (any Triticum species), rye, barley, oats or their crossbreeds; 'gluten-free' means at most 20 mg/kg as sold, and oats may only appear in gluten-free food if specially produced to avoid contamination and themselves at most 20 mg/kg.
notes: So spelt, einkorn, emmer, khorasan and durum are wheat for this purpose; buckwheat, rice, maize and chestnut are not gluten cereals but can be contaminated.

claim: The Farrand equation predicts flour water absorption from protein, starch damage and flour moisture only: WA = 68.26 + 0.878 × protein + 0.334 × damaged starch − 1.97 × moisture (all %). In 16 UK cultivars over two harvests it explained 83 % of the variance in absorption (86 % in a set of doubled-haploid lines); adding fibre traits raised this to about 90 %, the best single addition being total β-glucan (86.8 %).
conditions: UK white flours; farinograph absorption 'as is' (CCAT method 4); starch damage by Chopin SDmatic; protein N × 5.7
notes: The starch-damage unit is not stated: Farrand's original used Farrand units. With damaged starch in % of flour the equation returns low values (protein 11.5, damage 7, moisture 14 gives 53.1 %), so use it only with matched units or as a slope.

claim: Twenty Canadian hard red spring flour streams (protein 11.5–19.2 %, starch damage 15–89 Farrand units, absorption 60.5–79.2 %) gave farinograph absorption FA = 42.7 + 1.03 × protein + 0.248 × damaged starch (FU), r² = 0.993, standard error 0.42 points; starch damage alone gave FA = 58.0 + 0.207 × D (r² = 0.897). About 1 point of absorption came from each 4 Farrand units and from each 1 % protein; pentosan differences had no major influence.
conditions: protein N × 5.7; damaged starch in Farrand units

source.locator: Table V; p. 658 'Models for FA'; Table II
source.author: Tipples, Meredith & Holas

notes: Worked: protein 12 %, 25 FU gives 61.3 %; protein 14 %, 25 FU gives 63.3 %. The protein slope (≈ +1 point per % protein) is what Breadator uses to shift a flour type's default absorption.

claim: Baking absorption behaved differently from farinograph absorption: in a long remix process with 0.3 % malt it depended on gluten quality and protein (RBA = 22.8 + 10.9 × wet gluten/protein + 0.49 × protein, r² = 0.929), and starch damage lowered it by about 1 point per 13 Farrand units while raising farinograph absorption by 1 point per 4 units.
conditions: same 20 flour streams; remix baking test, 0.3 % malt
notes: Damaged starch is digested by amylase during long fermentation and gives its water back; a flour's farinograph absorption overstates what a long, malted process can carry.

claim: Approximate water binding of flour components: intact starch about 0.5 times its dry weight, damaged starch 3–4 times, proteins about 1.8 times, water-insoluble pentosans about 10 times and soluble pentosans about 11 times; arabinoxylan is 1.35–2.75 % of white flour (soluble part 0.3–1.4 %), and UK bread-making flours contain 10.5–12.5 % protein.
conditions: literature values compiled in the introduction
notes: Cites Kent & Evers 1994, Finnie & Atwell 2016, Guzmán 2015, Gebruers 2008.

claim: A water-distribution table for 100 g of flour assigns 22.05 g water to intact starch (63 g × 0.35 g/g), 11.38 g to damaged starch (6.5 g × 1.75), 14.0 g to water-unextractable arabinoxylan (1.4 g × 10), 3.0 g to water-extractable arabinoxylan (0.6 g × 5) and 17.28 g to gluten proteins (12.8 g × 1.35): 67.7 g in total, so arabinoxylans, only 2–3 % of the flour, hold about 25 % of the dough water.

source.locator: table on flour components and water absorption
source.author: BAKERpedia

notes: Coefficients differ from Lovegrove 2020 (science-flour-0050) and Feillet via Boucheham 2019 (science-flour-0052): see science-flour-0053.

claim: Water-holding capacity (1 g powder in 10 mL water, 30 min at 25 °C, centrifuged) was 5.31 g/g for maize, 4.84 for chickpea, 4.69 for faba bean, 2.48 for durum semolina and 2.36 for rice powder; the authors quote pentosans absorbing 15 times, gluten 2.15 times, native starch 0.44 times and damaged starch 2 times their weight.
notes: Centrifuge water-holding is not dough absorption; it ranks powders only. Component values cite Feillet 2000.

claim: Published water-binding coefficients for the same flour components disagree by a factor of up to two: damaged starch 1.75 g/g (BAKERpedia table), 2 (Feillet, via Boucheham 2019) or 3–4 times its weight (Kent & Evers, via Lovegrove 2020); gluten protein 1.35, 1.8 or 2.15 g/g; arabinoxylan 5–10 g/g, 10–11 g/g or 15 g/g, and 3.5–6.3 (extractable) and 6.7–9.9 g/g (unextractable) in an aleurone review. Summing components therefore cannot predict a flour's absorption; calibrated regressions (Farrand, Tipples) or measured absorption should be used.

source.locator: § on aleurone in bread (WEAX 3.5–6.3, WUAX 6.7–9.9 times their weight)
source.author: Lebert et al.

notes: Disagreement recorded with all values. Novita (novita-0506, novita-0641) quotes 15–20 times and up to 10 times for arabinoxylans.

claim: To match the farinograph consistency of a control, 0.5–2 % more water should be added per 1 % of arabinoxylan supplemented; the aleurone layer raises dough water absorption and lengthens development time.
Farinograph water absorption is conventionally reported on a 14 % moisture basis (AACCI 54-21.02, 500 BU), so flours of different moisture are compared at equal dry matter.

source.locator: §2 farinograph method ('All measurements were conducted on a 14% moisture basis')
source.author: Pradhan et al.

notes: Lovegrove 2020 instead reports 'as is' absorption: check the basis before comparing numbers.

claim: If dough consistency depends on total water per dry matter, absorption A₁₄ quoted at 14 % moisture converts to a flour of moisture M as A_M = (A₁₄ + 14) × (100 − M) / 86 − M. For A₁₄ = 60, a 12 %-moisture flour needs 63.7 % and a 15 %-moisture flour 58.1 %, about 1.86 points per point of moisture, close to the −1.97 moisture coefficient of the Farrand equation.
conditions: mass balance; same assumption as the 14 % moisture correction of the farinograph method
notes: Derived, not measured: algebra of constant water/dry-matter ratio, cross-checked against the empirical Farrand coefficient (science-flour-0047).

claim: Blend absorption is close to the mass-weighted mean of the components: with wheat at 61 % and rye at 84 % (midpoints of an industry table), the linear mean differs from the table's blend midpoints by −0.8 to +2.4 points across 90/10 to 10/90 blends, the largest gap (+2.4) at 80 % wheat / 20 % rye. A study of wholemeal flours used the same additivity to back-calculate absorption from 50:50 blends.
conditions: check of the linear rule against IREKS blend table (science-flour-0030)

source.locator: hydration_method.step_blend (check computed from IREKS dough-yield table)
source.author: Breadator synthesis

notes: Use ±2.5 points as blend uncertainty; rye-wheat blends with 10–40 % rye tend to sit above the linear mean.

claim: In one wheat flour, farinograph absorption was 62.8 % without salt, 59.7 % with 1 % NaCl and 58.9 % with 2 % NaCl (2 % KCl 58.2 %); in the dough, DSC starch gelatinization onset/peak/end were 60.17/70.83/79.83 °C without salt, 61.56/72.22/82.68 °C at 1 % and 61.73/72.90/84.93 °C at 2 % NaCl. Salt reduction also gave lower bread volume and faster firming.
conditions: salt % of flour; farinograph and alveograph; DSC on dough
notes: Farinograph tests are normally run without salt: a 2 % salt dough reaches the same consistency with about 4 points less water in this flour (single study).

claim: Without salt, the gelatinization peak of wheat starch rose 12 °C (from 62 to 74 °C) as water fell from 35 % to 25 %; NaCl shifted all thermal peaks upward, at 2 % NaCl the peak no longer depended much on water content, and above 45 % moisture the offset caused by 2 % NaCl was constant.
conditions: wheat starch, DSC, RVA, confocal microscopy
notes: Abstract only; the size of the salt offset is not given there.

claim: Vital wheat gluten is used at 1–4 % of flour in most yeast doughs and up to 12 % in high-fibre breads; 1 % added raises flour protein by about 0.6 points and dough absorption by about 1.5 points. Commercial vital gluten is roughly 73 % protein (78 % dry basis), 6 % fat, 6 % moisture and under 1 % ash, absorbs 140–180 % of its weight in water, and loses functionality if dried above 55 °C.
notes: The 0.6-point gain follows from the mixing rule: (100 × 11 + 1 × 73) / 101 = 11.61 %.

claim: USDA lists vital wheat gluten at 75.16 % protein, 8.2 % water, 1.0 % ash, 1.85 % fat and 13.79 % carbohydrate (81.9 % protein on dry matter).

EU nutrition labels calculate protein as total Kjeldahl nitrogen × 6.25 on the food as sold, whereas the Italian flour minima use N × 5.70 on dry matter; at 14.5 % moisture the legal minima of 9.00, 11.00 and 12.00 % correspond to about 8.4, 10.3 and 11.3 % on a label.
notes: The conversion is arithmetic (extrapolation from the two definitions). Ciqual prints both factors: T55 9.9 % (× 6.25) vs 9.03 % (Jones factor 5.7).

claim: Falling numbers do not average when flours are blended: they must first be converted to liquefaction numbers, LN = 6000 / (FN − 50), which mix linearly; for example a 50:50 blend of 200 s and 300 s flour has about 238 s, not 250 s.
notes: The 238 s result is computed here from the formula. Breadator's 'relative α-amylase activity' of a flour is its LN divided by the LN of a 320 s white wheat flour (22.2).

claim: Oat bran saturates at 1.6 g water per g dry bran (61.5 % water, aw 0.998), beyond which free water appears; replacing 20 % of white flour by bran pre-hydrated to saturation gave the best enriched bread (specific volume 4.21 cm³/g against 4.68 for white bread and 3.53 with under-hydrated bran). The 500 BU farinograph target did not predict absorption for these high-fibre doughs; the best dough was at 366 BU.
conditions: white pan bread; bran hydrated 2 h before mixing; water for the replaced flour reduced proportionally

claim: In a wholegrain wheat bread at equal dough consistency (500 FU, Micro-doughLAB), 100 flour took 55 water; with 5 % ground chia (95 flour) it took 80 and with 5 % psyllium husk (95 flour) 100. Removing the flour's own share (0.55 × 95 = 52.25), chia needed about 5.5 g and psyllium about 9.5 g of water per gram.
notes: Per-gram coefficients are derived here from the published formulas (one study, one dose).

claim: Psyllium (P. ovata) husk has a swelling factor of about 15 mL/g; in gluten-free breads 2.86–17.14 % psyllium was used with 82–118 % water and up to 10 % psyllium was added without adjusting water, rice breads with 0–4 % psyllium needed 90–110 g water per 100 g flour, and in wheat bread about 3.5 % psyllium at 75 % hydration gave the best physical properties.

source.locator: swelling (Sharma & Koul 1986); bread applications (Fratelli 2018, Mancebo 2015, Mironeasa & Codină 2023)
source.author: Strkalj et al.

notes: 'Up to 10 % without adjusting water' (gluten-free) disagrees with the 9.5 g/g needed at equal consistency in wheat dough (science-flour-0065).

claim: Flaxseed mucilage binds 1600–3000 g water per 100 g of solids and makes up about 6 % of the seed; chia yields about 7 % mucilage and flax slightly over 9 %. In wheat dough 5 % chia flour did not change farinograph absorption but 15 % raised it, pre-hydrating chia raised absorption and shortened development, and both flax and chia reduce extensibility; sensory acceptance holds up to 10–15 % seed addition.
notes: Mucilage binding from Puligundla & Lim 2022 §1–2.

claim: A German baking lexicon gives guide values for soaker water (g water per 100 g solids): 50 for nuts, pumpkin, sesame and sunflower seeds and fresh bread; 100 for cracked buckwheat, spelt, rye or wheat, oat flakes, durum semolina, quinoa and soy; 150 for whole linseed and corn grits; 200 for wheat bran, cracked linseed and dried old bread in cold water; 300 for old bread with boiling water; 400 for potato flakes; 1000 for whole psyllium seed and 2000–4000 for psyllium husk. Soakers are mixed 1:1 to 1:2 at 10–30 °C and rest 4–20 h (or 8–12 h at 6–8 °C); coarse meal should not exceed 30–60 % of the cereal products.
notes: These are saturation (soaker) ratios, higher than the extra water at equal dough consistency for psyllium (≈ 9.5 g/g, science-flour-0065).

claim: An industry handbook distinguishes soaked grain (dough yield 160–250, water 10–50 °C, 1–16 h, up to 60 % of the flour, starch swollen, enzymes active), hot-soaked grain (dough yield 200–250, water 60–80 °C, held 60–70 °C for 2–4 h, up to 20 %, starch partly gelatinized) and boiled grain (dough yield 350–400, 100 °C, about 95 °C for 2–3 h, up to 15 %, starch gelatinized, enzymes inactive).
conditions: coarse grain for mixed and wholemeal breads

source.locator: overview table 'Soaked grain, hot soaked grain and boiled grain'
source.author: IREKS GmbH

notes: Dough yield 200 = 1 part water per part grain; 350–400 = 2.5–3 parts.

claim: Breadator default for common-wheat flour farinograph absorption when no mill value is known: A₁₄ ≈ 59 + 8 × (ash % dry matter − 0.55) + 1.0 × (protein − 11.5), with an uncertainty of ±3 points. The intercept matches a measured type-530 white flour (60.6 %) and an unsalted flour (62.8 %, 58.9 % with 2 % salt); the ash slope reproduces the +8 points between French T55 and T150 reference recipes (62 vs 70 % water) and the +5.5 to +8 points between refined and wholemeal flours of one mill; the protein slope is Tipples' coefficient.
conditions: T. aestivum flours, farinograph 500 BU, 14 % moisture basis
notes: Not fitted to a dataset: anchored on science-flour-0029, -0058, -0006, -0035 and -0048. Replace by the mill's farinograph value whenever available.

claim: Breadator cold-retard tolerance classes: high (strong flours, W above about 250 or protein ≥ 12.5 %): up to 48–72 h in the fridge; medium (bread flours of medium strength, wholemeal wheat, rye and rye-wheat doughs): 12–24 h, up to 48 h with care; low (weak or very extensible gluten: einkorn, emmer, white spelt, pastry flours): up to 12 h; gluten-free doughs: no gluten structure to lose, limit set by fermentation and starch only.
conditions: dough at 4–6 °C; sourdough or reduced yeast
notes: Reasoning: fermentation time tolerated rises with W (science-flour-0043); fridge proofs of about 24 h are standard and still good at 48 h (breadcode-0611); pizza dough keeps up to 7 days cold (breadcode-1323); weak ancient-wheat gluten has low stability and high gliadin/glutenin ratios (science-flour-0023, -0026, -0027); high α-amylase flours give damp, weak doughs over long times (science-flour-0032). No study measured retard limits per flour type.

claim: Yudane made by mixing flour with boiling water 1:1 and keeping it one day at 5 °C was added at 20 % and 40 % of the flour: farinograph water absorption for bread making rose from 68 % (control) to 71 % and 74 %, final proof from 84.0 to 86.0 and 86.5 min, while gas retention fell from 130 to 119 and 108 mL and specific loaf volume from 5.99 to 5.79 and 5.37 mL/g; bread moisture rose from 45.3 to 45.7 and 46.3 %.
conditions: bread flour 12.2 % protein, 0.39 % ash (13.5 % moisture basis); 5 % sugar, 5 % shortening, 2 % salt; no-time dough
notes: Absorption shift = +0.15 points per % of the flour scalded (3 points per 20 %). Novita's tables (novita-0120, novita-0369) reproduce these values.

claim: In the same breads, water-soluble total saccharides rose from 49.0 mg/g (control) to 73.0 (20 % yudane) and 96.7 mg/g (40 %), and maltose from 24.1 to 33.9 and 47.2 mg/g: yudane 40 % roughly doubled sugars and maltose.
notes: Gelatinized starch is open to flour amylases during the cold rest and the dough stage.

claim: Yudane bread was softer and staled more slowly: initial crumb hardness fell from 1.53 (control) to 1.38 and 1.19 × 10³ N/m² at 20 and 40 % yudane, limiting hardness from 7.42 to 6.96 and 6.67 × 10³ N/m², the staling rate constant from 0.97 to 0.92 and 0.89 × 10⁻² h⁻¹ and the retrogradation rate constant from 2.68 to 2.16 and 2.07 × 10⁻² h⁻¹.
conditions: crumb stored at 20 °C (limiting hardness after 10 days at 4.7 °C)
notes: The authors attribute it to higher crumb moisture, more sugars and amylase-modified gelatinized starch.

claim: A 1:1 boiling-water yudane mixed 4 min at low speed ended at 55 ± 1 °C and was stored one day at 5 °C; used at 10 % and 20 % of the flour with total water held at 68 % (59.5 and 51 % outside the yudane), it needed 65 min final proof against 60 min, and at 20 °C storage the hardening rate constant fell from 0.89 to 0.87 and 0.65 × 10⁻² h⁻¹ and the limiting hardness from 7.67 to 6.29 and 5.65 kPa.
notes: Unlike Yamauchi 2014, this study did not raise total water with the yudane.

claim: Crumb hardening of yudane and control breads followed H(t) = H_L − (H_L − H_0) · exp(−A (θm − θ)³ t), with θ the storage temperature; θm, the temperature at which hardening stops, was 67.6 °C for the control and 61.3 and 58.8 °C for 10 and 20 % yudane, with A = 7.20 × 10⁻⁸, 1.10 × 10⁻⁷ and 1.22 × 10⁻⁷ h⁻¹ °C⁻³. Hardening slowed as storage temperature rose, and yudane bread hardened more slowly at every temperature.
notes: A first-order model with a cubic temperature term, not an Avrami model.

claim: Wheat starch gelatinized in a 98–100 °C water bath for 10 min and used to replace 20 % of the flour let pizza dough carry 1.04 g water per g dry flour-starch instead of 0.82 g/g at unchanged viscoelasticity (G′, G″ and yield stress rose with starch replacement at each water content); crust density was unchanged and the crumb stayed wetter.
conditions: pizza dough models and samples (flour 80 + starch 20, water 80 vs flour 100, water 60)
notes: (1.04 − 0.82) / 0.20 = 1.1 g extra water per g of fully gelatinized starch; in baker's terms +20 points for 20 % gelatinized starch, i.e. about +1 point per % of flour.

claim: Flour gelatinized at 90 °C and added at 5, 10 and 20 % (w/w) moderately raised dough viscoelasticity and lowered freezing and melting enthalpies of dough water, acting as a binder that traps water; bread texture changed insignificantly.
notes: Abstract only; no numbers for water absorption or volume.

claim: Wheat starch heated in excess water (water:starch 2–4 v/w) to the DSC conclusion temperature Tc (65.6–67.5 °C) still had 1.7–2.8 J/g of gelatinization enthalpy left; none remained after heating to Te (71.0–73.6 °C). Gelatinization of wheat and maize starch had not started at the DSC onset and was not complete at Tc; below about 67 % water the endotherm reflects limited swelling rather than full gelatinization.
conditions: RVA pre-heating to Tc or Te, then DSC at 10 °C/min
notes: Rice starch: To 58.9–60.0, Tp 64.8–65.8, Tc 69.6–72.4 °C over water:starch 0.5–4; maize: To 64.3–65.8, Tp 68.7–71.1, Tc 72.5–77.2 °C (Table 1).

claim: When total water is below about 66 %, wheat starch gelatinizes by more than one mechanism: the excess-water endotherm (G) shrinks and a higher-temperature melting endotherm (M1) appears, spread over up to 40–50 °C instead of 10–15 °C; at water:starch 1:1 the total enthalpy was 2.84–3.00 cal/g dry starch, and enthalpy fell quickly once the starch was held above 52 °C.
notes: M.S. thesis; J/g = cal/g × 4.184.

claim: Combining the residual enthalpy left at Tc (1.7–2.8 J/g, Wang 2018) with the full gelatinization enthalpy of wheat starch (about 11.9–12.6 J/g, Yost 1985) suggests that wheat starch in excess water is only about 76–86 % gelatinized at 66–67 °C and needs about 71–74 °C to gelatinize completely. A tangzhong held at 65 °C is therefore mostly but not fully gelatinized; heating it to 75–80 °C completes it.
conditions: starch in excess water (tangzhong 1:3 to 1:5); different starch samples and methods combined
notes: Disagreement on the target temperature: the classic tangzhong stops at 65 °C (novita-0614, novita-0846) and Novita estimates about 90 % gelatinized there but now targets 75–80 °C (novita-0013); BAKERpedia heats a 1:5 paste to 80 °C (science-flour-0086).

claim: Sugars raise the gelatinization onset of wheat starch (DSC, starch:solution 1:2): from 60.71 °C in water to 65.80, 72.23, 82.35 and 98.49 °C in 15, 30, 45 and 60 % (w/w) sucrose solutions; glucose 64.31, 69.15 and 77.49 °C at 15–45 %; fructose 63.31, 68.35, 75.96 and 85.38 °C at 15–60 %. Changing water alone (matched controls) left the onset at 60.70–61.57 °C.
conditions: wheat starch (25 % amylose); sugar concentration in the solution phase
notes: Allan et al. 2020 (same lab, wheat starch onset 60.78 °C in water) found +3.54, +11.50, +19.20 and +28.86 °C in 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 M sucrose. A 20 % sugar sweet dough at 60 % hydration has about 25 % sugar in its water phase.

claim: Starch melting temperature versus water fraction follows a Flory–Huggins form, 1/Tm − 1/Tm° = (R/ΔHu)(vu/vw)(Φw − χΦw²), extended to sugar solutions by replacing Φw with an effective water fraction weighted by hydroxyl-group density; for wheat starch Tm° = 473 K. At starch mass fractions of 0.5–0.7 DSC shows two endotherms, at 0.8 and above a single one.
notes: Wheat coefficients come from an earlier paper by the same group; not used as a calculator formula here because the molar-volume ratio is not given in the text read.

claim: Amylograph gelatinization began at 54.6 °C for wholemeal rye flour, 56.1 °C for white wheat flour, 58.6 °C for wholemeal spelt, 59.8 °C for buckwheat, 61.0 °C for barley, 63.5 °C for wholemeal wheat and 65.6 °C for sorghum; peak viscosity was 495 AU for rye against 540 for white wheat and 3702 for buckwheat.
notes: Rye starch gelatinizes earliest and rye has the most α-amylase: why rye crumb needs acid (science-flour-0032).

claim: Gelatinization ranges quoted for cereal starches: wheat, barley and rye 51–60 °C, triticale 55–62 °C, corn 62–72 °C, rice and sorghum 68–78 °C, potato 60–65 °C, tapioca 67–70 °C; amylose and amylopectin start to solubilize at about 70 °C and 90 °C, and native starch takes up only 30–40 % of its dry weight as moisture. Sugars, salts and polyols raise the temperature needed.
notes: These ranges sit 5–10 °C below DSC onsets measured for wheat starch (60.7–61.7 °C, science-flour-0058, -0082) and rice (about 59 °C, science-flour-0079): method dependent.

claim: A water-roux ('tangzhong') formula precooks 6.25 % of the flour with five times its weight of water (31.25 parts), heated to 80 °C for 2–5 min until a viscous paste forms and then chilled; the paste is 37.5 % of flour weight in a dough of 75 % total hydration.
notes: Cites Parenti et al. 2019 for higher W, larger volume and slower staling (full text not accessible here).

claim: A Latvian rye scald: rye flour with 1 % diastatic rye malt mixed 10 min with water at 96 °C at dough yield 350 (1:2.5), saccharified 90 min while cooling from 75 to 60 °C, then fermented with lactic bacteria (55 → 35 °C over 20 h): pH fell from 6.92 to 3.61 and TTA rose from 1.4 to 12.5. Rye bread with the fermented scald was 46 % softer (2.30 vs 4.29 N) but smaller (1.61 vs 1.85 cm³/g, porosity 58.8 vs 67.0 %); in hull-less barley bread the scald increased hardness (22.28 vs 17.97 N).
notes: Scalding is described as pouring 90–98 °C water over flour, with saccharification in 2–4 h at 62–65 °C.

claim: Wholegrain rye scalds (about 1:1.5 flour:water at 92–96 °C, mixed to about 75 °C, cooled to 55 °C over 90 min) reached 11.8 g/100 g maltose without malt and up to 18.2 g/100 g with 1.5 % high-activity malt; another bakery scald made 42.9 % of the bread's flour, held 25–28 g/100 g dry matter maltose before and after fermentation, and its lactic acid rose from 0.27 to about 3.7 g/100 g dry matter after 24–48 h at 30 °C.

source.locator: Table 2 (6.00 kg flour + 9.00 kg water at 92 °C in the scald, 8.00 kg flour in the dough), Tables 3 and 5
source.author: Murniece et al.

notes: Scald share computed from printed amounts: 6.00 / (6.00 + 8.00) = 42.9 %. Enzyme optima are cited in Murniece 2024 (§1).

claim: A Brühstück mixes coarse meal, flakes or old bread with boiling water at about 1:1 to 1:3 and rests at least 2–6 h (or 8–12 h at 6–8 °C after cooling); coarse meal scalded this way should not exceed 30–50 % of the cereal products because its starch is already gelatinized, and scalded dried old bread binds about three times its weight. A Kochstück is boiled at about 100 °C, which denatures all grain enzymes, and binds much water.

For hot-soaked grain, 10–20 % of the coarse grain is scalded with the same weight of boiling water, ending near 60 °C with partly gelatinized starch and active amylases, and stands about 3 h; it should be reduced or omitted with sprout-damaged grain. Boiled grain (about 15 % of the coarse grain, 92–95 °C) must be counted in the dough yield and used within 2–3 days. Too much soaker gives water streaks, sticky crumb, hollows and lower volume; the right amount gives a moister crumb, better keeping and faster final proof.
conditions: coarse grain for mixed and wholemeal breads

source.locator: pages 'Hot soaked grain', 'Boiled grain', 'Effects on the baked goods properties', 'Effects on the dough properties'
source.author: IREKS GmbH

claim: Published values for the water a scald adds at equal dough consistency disagree: a 1:1 boiling-water yudane raised absorption by 0.15 points per % of flour scalded (68 → 71 → 74 % at 20 and 40 %); another 1:1 yudane study kept total water unchanged at 68 % for 10 and 20 %; fully gelatinized starch allowed about +1 point per % of flour (+1.1 g water per g); Novita advises no extra water below 10 % scalded and about +2 points per further 10 %, and elsewhere says a 30–40 % tangzhong raises farinograph absorption by less than 2 %.
conditions: wheat breads; scald share as % of total flour
notes: Disagreement recorded with all values: novita-0129, novita-0514, novita-0120. The spread follows the degree of gelatinization: a 1:1 yudane cools to about 55 °C (science-flour-0075) and is only partly gelatinized; a starch cooked at 98–100 °C is fully gelatinized.

claim: Studies and creator advice disagree on scald share, softness and staling: in Yamauchi 2014 crumb was softest and staled slowest at the highest level tested (40 % yudane), whereas Novita reports a thesis in which 10–20 % tangzhong was softest and shares above 30 % accelerated staling and cut volume, and recommends 10–30 % (about 20 % for milk breads).
notes: Disagreement with novita-0005, novita-0015, novita-0481, novita-0495 and novita-0826 (Ke Yuwen 2004 thesis, not read). The thesis doughs were near 60 % hydration (novita-0826); Yamauchi raised water with the yudane.

claim: A 1:1 flour:boiling-water yudane does not stay hot: in a measured process it ended mixing at 55 ± 1 °C, below the 60–62 °C onset of wheat-starch gelatinization in excess water, so only part of its starch gelatinizes; Novita's statement that a 1:1 scald 'still gelatinizes well' holds only if the mix stays above about 65 °C (pre-warmed bowl, water poured first, fast mixing).
notes: Disagreement with novita-0764 and novita-0803; consistent with novita-0754 and novita-0804 (keep it above 65 °C). Onsets from science-flour-0058 and science-flour-0082.

claim: Rye scald practice differs by source: Novita cites 10–30 % of the flour at 1:2–1:3 flour:boiling water, cooled 4–12 h to 25–30 °C and 85–100 % gelatinized; an industry handbook limits hot-soaked grain to 20 % and boiled grain to 15 %; a German lexicon allows coarse meal scalds up to 30–50 % of cereal products at 1:1–1:3; and a published Latvian rye bread scalds 42.9 % of its flour at 1:1.5 (another study 1:2.5).
notes: Disagreement with novita-0451; Plötzblog values in science-flour-0089, IREKS in science-flour-0069 and -0090.

claim: Scald water accounting: with total flour F, scalded share s and scald ratio r (water per flour), the scald holds F_s = s·F flour and W_s = r·F_s water; the water left for the dough is W_total − W_s − W_other stages and must not be negative. Water lost while cooking is measured by weighing flour plus water before and the paste after (loss = W1 − W2) and added back. Example: 1000 g flour, 20 % scalded at 1:5 puts 1000 g of water in the scald, more than a 75 % dough holds in total.
notes: Mass balance (counting scald flour and water in totals) as advised by novita-0138 and novita-0128; weighing method novita-0515; Novita's remark that 1:5 cannot reach useful scald shares (novita-0124) follows directly.

claim: Vital-gluten dose to raise a flour's protein from P_f to a target P_t with gluten of protein P_g (all as-is %, same nitrogen factor): G = F × (P_t − P_f) / (P_g − P_t). Example: 1000 g of 11.0 % flour to 13.0 % with 75 % gluten needs 1000 × 2.0 / 62.0 = 32.3 g, not the 2.7 % that a naive '1 % gluten = 0.75 % protein' would suggest; on a dry-matter basis (flour 14 % and gluten 8.2 % moisture) the same target needs 32.6 g.
conditions: mixing rule; requires P_f < P_t < P_g
notes: Mass-balance algebra; consistent with BAKERpedia's '+0.6 protein point per 1 % gluten' (science-flour-0060): 100 g at 11 % + 1 g at 73 % gives 11.61 %.

claim: Protein targets for flours by bread type gathered from creators and references: about 10.5–11.5 % for steamed buns and mantou; 11–12 % (all-purpose) for soft enriched rolls and lighter fried doughs; about 12 % for baguette; 12–13 % for doughnuts and 13 % for soft Japanese-style pan loaves and enriched rolls; 11.5–13.5 % for US bread flour; 13.5 % or more for 100 % whole wheat; about 14 % high-gluten flour for bagels and chewy hearth breads.
conditions: protein as on US labels (about 14 % moisture basis); creator rules
notes: From novita-0772, novita-0267, novita-0380, novita-0256, novita-0845, novita-0552, novita-0032, science-flour-0021 and science-flour-0022. French practice reaches good baguettes at about 11.5 % (N × 6.25, as is; science-flour-0005) and UK bread flours run 10.5–12.5 % (science-flour-0050).

claim: Rye grain is about 86.5 % starchy endosperm, 10 % bran and 3.5 % germ; arabinoxylans are the main water-binding polymers in rye dough and govern its rheology and gas retention. North American rye breads typically contain about 20 % rye flour, whereas 100 % rye loaves are common in Europe.
notes: Rye proteins do not form a gluten network; the structure comes from pentosans and gelatinized starch protected by acid.

claim: Stone-milled flours used for sourdough breads had: modern wheat 11.3 % protein, 1.48 % ash, 10.45 % total fibre; spelt 15.87 / 1.98 / 10.1; emmer 15.99 / 1.87 / 9.58; khorasan 11.49 / 1.50 / 9.85 (moisture 10.7–11.3 %).
conditions: Serbian stone-milled flours; dough water set to 400 BU
notes: High-extraction (near wholemeal) flours, judging by ash.

claim: In French practice T45, the whitest flour, is used mostly for cakes and pastry; T55 for everyday white bread and viennoiserie; T65, the best-selling type, for most breads including the 'baguette de tradition française' and pain de campagne; T80 ('farine bise') for pain bis; T110 ('semi-complète') for semi-wholemeal bread; T150 for wholemeal ('complet', 'intégral') bread.

source.locator: p. 4 'Quel type pour quelle utilisation ?'; p. 2 (dénominations bise and semi-complète)
source.author: ANMF / CNBPF

notes: The vocational course of the Académie de Versailles gives the same uses (T45 pâtisserie; T55 panification and viennoiserie; T110–T150 speciality breads).

claim: The DIN 10355 table describes uses: wheat 405 is the preferred household flour for fine pastry and cakes; 550 is 'backstark' (strong in baking), for fine-pored doughs, light breads and rolls; 812 for light mixed breads; 1050 for mixed breads; 1600 for dark mixed breads; rye 815 rarely, for light rye breads; 997 and 1150 for mixed breads; 1370 and 1740 are the typical bakers' flours for rye and mixed rye breads.

US rye flours are graded light (patent flour), medium (straight grade) and dark (clear flour): 'dark rye' is the high-protein, high-ash clear stream left after the patent is taken, not a wholemeal flour.
notes: Explains why the USDA 'dark rye' row (15.9 % protein, 23.8 % fibre, 2.5 % ash) differs from wholemeal rye (about 11 % protein on dry matter, science-flour-0029), and why Ciqual's T170 row, copied from it, is not a French wholemeal rye (science-flour-0009).

claim: A French vocational course pairs flour types with approximate extraction rates: T45 about 70 %, T55 75 %, T65 80 %, T80 82 %, T110 85 % and T150 90 %, rye T170 being wholemeal; an Italian study milled type 0 at 72 %, type 1 at 80 % and integrale at 100 % extraction.
conditions: teaching material; extraction depends on the wheat and the mill

source.locator: p. 2, table 'Types / Taux de cendres / % d'extraction'
source.author: Académie de Versailles, Métiers de l'alimentation

notes: Italian figures from Di Renzo et al. 2023 (science-flour-0028).

claim: Novita quotes about 23 mg of maltose per gram in a yudane 40 bread; the cited study measured 47.2 mg/g in yudane 40 bread against 24.1 mg/g in the control, so 23 mg/g is the increase (47.2 − 24.1 = 23.1), not the content.
notes: Disagreement with novita-0476; novita-0114 (maltose about doubled at 40 %) agrees with the table.
